# Abstract

Stretching across 245k km² of the Caspian Depression, the Lower Volga contrasts the 400 km Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain and the Volga Delta with the dry Kalmyk-Yergeni and Trans-Volga steppes on either side. From a few thousand Mesolithic and Neolithic fishermen at Varfolomeyevka, Kairshak, Tenteksor and Dzhangar (3k in 10000BC; 13k in 5000BC) [@yudin2004varfolomeyevka; @baratskov2015itogi; @smagin2018mikrolitov; @vybornov2022khronologiya] and Copper Age herders at Khvalynsk I-II and Maksimovka I (21,5k in 4000BC) [@agapov1990khvalynskiy; @tsibin2019maksimovka], numbers rose with wheeled steppe herding [@shishlina2008reconstruction; @borisov2019palaeosols] to 95k during the Late Bronze Age Srubnaya village expansion (>850 northern valley villages in 1500BC) [@malov2008nizhneye; @lopatin2014nachalo] and 97k under the Middle Sarmatian Aorsi confederacy (150AD) [@balabanova2009khronologicheskiye; @skripkin2012chislennosti; @pererva2015istorii; @krivosheev2021chelovek]. In the Middle Ages, the delta and floodplain twice became the heart of large steppe states: excavations at Khazar Itil (Semibugry/Barany Bugor) and Pre-Mongol Saksin (Samosdelka) point to a regional population of 138k in 900AD and 104k in 1200AD [@vasilyev2015saksin; @vasilyev2020samosdelka; @solovyev2022semibugry], while Golden Horde town and village surveys at Ukek, Bagaevskoye, Beldzhamen, Sarai al-Jadid (Tsarevskoye), Sarai Batu (Selitrennoye) and Hajji-Tarkhan show a medieval peak of 375k (308k-450k) in 1340AD [@yegorov1985geografiya; @nedashkovsky2010goroda; @zeleneev2018selitrennom; @pigarev2021topografii; @nedashkovsky2022predmety; @shigapov2022selishch]. Timur's 1395-1396 sack of the floodplain cities cut the population to 87k in 1400AD, and after a brief Nogai and Astrakhan Tatar recovery to 130k in 1550AD, the 1557-1558 famine and plague reduced numbers to 68k in 1600AD [@moiseev2015stepnyye; @trepavlov2016nogayskoy]. Oirat-Kalmyk migration and Russian garrison towns lifted the total to 245k by 1700AD [@tepkeev2025dzhungarskiye; @muzraev2025uchastiye], before 18th- and 19th-century peasant and Volga German farming settlement, the arrival of the Inner Bukey Kazakh Horde and railway building carried the population to 3,65M by 1900AD [@kabuzan1963narodonaseleniye; @pleve1998nemetskiye; @doenninghaus2011nemetskikh; @solovyov2013saratovskoy; @brylyov2018volgogradskoy; @ochirov2008tyurkoyazychnyye; @okonova2012migratsii; @kyshpanakov2026kalmyki; @belousov2019bukeyevskoy; @pirova2020tatarakh; @troynitsky1904saratov; @troynitsky1904astrakhan].

# Background

The Lower Volga (~ 245k km²) is shaped by the sharp contrast between the 400 km-long Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain and fan-shaped Volga Delta and the surrounding dry steppes and semi-deserts of the Caspian Depression (Figure \ref{fig:hero}). We divide the territory into five regions.

The first region is the Volga Delta and north-western Caspian coast (22k km²), taking in the main delta channels (Bolda, Buzan and Bakhtemir), Baer knolls (*Berovskiye bugry*) and coastal lagoons. Its main sites include Seroglazovka, Kairshak, Tenteksor, Khazar Itil at Semibugry/Barany Bugor, Samosdelka (Saksin/Summerkent), Golden Horde Hajji-Tarkhan (Shareny Bugor), Krasnoyarskoye and Russian Astrakhan and Krasny Yar [@vasilyev2020samosdelka; @solovyev2022semibugry]. The second region is the Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain (18k km²), a 15-45 km-wide wooded and meadow belt between the Volgograd (Tsaritsyn) bend and the top of the delta. This floodplain hosted the capitals of the Golden Horde - Sarai al-Jadid (Sarai Berke at Tsarevskoye Gorodishche) and Sarai Batu (Sarai al-Mahrusa at Selitrennoye Gorodishche), together with the royal tombs of Ak-Sarai at Lapas - as well as the later Russian towns of Tsaritsyn, Chyorny Yar, Yenotayevsk and Tsarev [@yegorov1985geografiya; @nedashkovsky2010goroda; @pigarev2021topografii].

The third region covers the Saratov-Volgograd right bank and northern Trans-Volga (Zavolzhye) valley corridor (60k km²), where forest-steppe gives way to dry steppe along the Volga and the Medveditsa, Ilovlya, Bolshoy Irgiz and Yeruslan rivers. Key settlements include prehistoric Varfolomeyevka, Khvalynsk I-II, Khlopkov Bugor and Pokrovsk, the Golden Horde towns of Ukek (Uvekskoye Gorodishche, with its 53-village farming district including Bagaevskoye Selishche) and Beldzhamen (Vodyanskoye Gorodishche), the Russian towns of Saratov, Kamyshin, Volsk and Khvalynsk and the 18th-19th century Volga German *Bergseite* and *Wiesenseite* colonies [@yudin2004varfolomeyevka; @nedashkovsky2022predmety; @shigapov2022selishch; @pleve1998nemetskiye]. The fourth region covers the Kalmyk Steppe, Yergeni Hills and Sarpa Lakes (75k km²), the right-bank dry steppes south of the Volga-Don portage along the Yergeni ridge, the Sarpa lakes and the Black Lands (*Chyornye Zemli*). It contains Neolithic Dzhangar, Bronze Age Manych Catacomb and Lola burial mounds, 17th-19th century Kalmyk *uluses*, the Moravian settlement of Sarepta and Elista [@koltsov2005mezolit; @shishlina2008reconstruction; @tepkeev2012kalmyki; @okonova2012migratsii]. The fifth region is the Astrakhan-Volgograd Trans-Volga (Zavolzhye) and Ryn-Caspian Steppe (70k km²), the left-bank semi-desert steppes between the Akhtuba valley and the Volga-Ural (Yaik) watershed around Lakes Elton and Baskunchak and the Bolshoy and Maly Uzen rivers; it served in turn as 16th-century Nogai and 17th-18th century Torghut-Kalmyk winter pastures and as the territory of the 19th-century Inner (Bukey) Kazakh Horde and Novouzensk steppes [@trepavlov2016nogayskoy; @belousov2019bukeyevskoy].

# Methodology

Population estimates across the Lower Volga combine archaeological survey data with historical registers and census returns. For the Mesolithic, Neolithic and Copper Age (10000-3500BC), A. V. Baratskov [@baratskov2015itogi], V. A. Smagin [@smagin2018mikrolitov], A. A. Vybornov et al. [@vybornov2022khronologiya], P. M. Koltsov [@koltsov2005mezolit] and A. I. Yudin [@yudin2004varfolomeyevka] provide excavated pit-house floor areas (30-60 m² at Varfolomeyevka) and AMS radiocarbon series (89 dates by 2015 and more than 200 by 2022), while S. A. Agapov et al. [@agapov1990khvalynskiy] and V. A. Tsibin and A. A. Shalapinin [@tsibin2019maksimovka] establish Copper Age cemetery cohorts (201 skeletons at Khvalynsk I-II). For the Bronze and Early Iron Ages (3500BC-400AD), northern valley settlement inventories (>850 Srubnaya villages) [@malov2008nizhneye; @lopatin2014nachalo] and buried-soil studies [@borisov2019palaeosols; @krivosheev2021chelovek] are paired with skeletal mortality series analysed by M. A. Balabanova [@balabanova2000antropologiya; @balabanova2009khronologicheskiye; @balabanova2013detskaya; @balabanova2015skripkin] and E. V. Pererva and E. G. Zubareva [@pererva2015istorii] and with A. S. Skripkin's [@skripkin2012chislennosti] comparison of Sarmatian pastures against historical Kalmyk herd capacities.

For the medieval delta and floodplain towns (740-1460AD), D. V. Vasilyev [@vasilyev2015saksin; @vasilyev2020samosdelka], E. D. Zilivinskaya [@zilivinskaya2014ocherki] and D. S. Solovyev et al. [@solovyev2022semibugry] estimate urban populations for Khazar Itil (Semibugry/Barany Bugor and Samosdelka) and Pre-Mongol Saksin. For the Golden Horde heartland, V. L. Yegorov [@yegorov1985geografiya], G. A. Fyodorov-Davydov [@fyodorovdavydov1994goroda], Yu. A. Zeleneev and E. M. Pigarev [@zeleneev2018selitrennom; @pigarev2021topografii], L. F. Nedashkovsky [@nedashkovsky2000ukek; @nedashkovsky2010goroda; @nedashkovsky2022predmety; @nedashkovsky2022izdeliya] and M. B. Shigapov [@shigapov2022selishch] document built-up urban areas (Ukek >205 ha, Beldzhamen 50 ha, Tsarevskoye >400 ha core and >1k ha with suburbs, Selitrennoye ~ 380 ha core and ~ 1k ha with suburbs) and surrounding agricultural villages (53 *selishcha* around Ukek and 17 around Tsarevskoye).

For the post-Jochid and early modern era (1460-1700AD), archival studies by M. V. Moiseev [@moiseev2015stepnyye], I. V. Zaitsev [@zaitsev2006astrakhanskoye], A. V. Syzranov [@syzranov2014astrakhani], V. V. Trepavlov [@trepavlov2016nogayskoy], V. T. Tepkeev [@tepkeev2012kalmyki; @tepkeev2025dzhungarskiye] and N. L. Muzraev [@muzraev2025uchastiye] establish Great Horde, Astrakhan Tatar, Nogai *san* and Kalmyk *kibitka* counts (35k-45k tents, or 160k-210k people) alongside Russian *Razryadny Prikaz* fortress censuses. For the 18th and 19th centuries (1700-1900AD), V. M. Kabuzan [@kabuzan1963narodonaseleniye], I. R. Pleve [@pleve1998nemetskiye], V. Dönninghaus [@doenninghaus2011nemetskikh], V. Yu. Solovyov [@solovyov2013saratovskoy], V. A. Brylyov [@brylyov2018volgogradskoy], U. B. Ochirov [@ochirov2008tyurkoyazychnyye], L. V. Okonova [@okonova2012migratsii], V. A. Kyshpanakov [@kyshpanakov2026kalmyki], S. S. Belousov [@belousov2019bukeyevskoy], R. N. Pirova [@pirova2020tatarakh] and N. A. Troynitsky [@troynitsky1904saratov; @troynitsky1904astrakhan] provide counts from the ten Imperial *revizii* (1719-1858), the 1764-1767 Volga German colony registers, the 1771 Kalmyk exodus records, the Inner (Bukey) Kazakh Horde censuses and the 1897 Census across Saratov and Astrakhan Governorates.^[All archived full-text academic PDFs cited in this review are stored locally in histmap/1.data_raw/population_regional/POLARIS/pontic_steppe_and_lower_volga/papers/.]

# Results

## From Early Foragers to Sarmatian Nomads

### The Mesolithic, Neolithic and Copper Age

Investigated by P. M. Koltsov [@koltsov2005mezolit] and V. A. Smagin [@smagin2018mikrolitov], the Mesolithic of the Northern Caspian lowlands and Volga-Ural sands (10000-6800 cal BC) is represented by the Seroglazovka and Istay cultures (Seroglazovka, Zhe-Kalgan, Kairshak V), characterised by geometric flint microliths (segments, trapezes and parallelograms traced across the Lower Volga by Smagin [@smagin2018mikrolitov]). Small mobile bands (15-35 persons per camp) hunted saiga, kulan and onager and fished along delta channels, with regional population growing gradually from 3k (10000BC, density 0,012 persons/km²) to 5,2k (8000BC).

As documented by A. V. Baratskov [@baratskov2015itogi] and A. A. Vybornov et al. [@vybornov2022khronologiya], the radiocarbon dataset for the Steppe Volga Neolithic expanded from 12 dates prior to 2007 to 89 dates by 2015 and more than 200 AMS dates by 2022, establishing the Northern Caspian and Lower Volga as one of the earliest pottery-making regions in Western Eurasia. At the Kairshak sites (6800-5800 cal BC, including Kairshak I-III, Baibek and Kugat IV), flat-bottomed incised pottery and geometric microliths yielded AMS dates of 7950-7930 BP (6800-6500 cal BC) alongside light surface dwellings (15-28 m²) [@baratskov2015itogi]. At Varfolomeyevka (Orlovka Culture, 6000-5000 cal BC), excavated by A. I. Yudin [@yudin2004varfolomeyevka] in the Saratov Trans-Volga, a 3,5 m cultural deposit across Layer 3 (6200-5800 cal BC), Layer 2B (5600-5300 cal BC) and Layer 2A (5200-4900 cal BC) [@baratskov2015itogi] preserved permanent multi-room semi-subterranean pit-houses (*poluzemlyanki* of 30-60 m²) that housed 60-100 residents per phase. At Tenteksor I and Dzhangar (5600-4800 cal BC in Kalmykia, upper layer dated to 6564 +/- 44 BP/c. 5500 cal BC [@koltsov2005mezolit; @baratskov2015itogi]), communities settled around freshwater limans in sub-rectangular pit-dwellings (35-50 m²), raising regional population to 9,8k (6000BC) and 13k (5000BC).

During the Copper Age (4800-3500 cal BC), the cemeteries of Khvalynsk I (158 skeletons) and Khvalynsk II (43 skeletons) [@agapov1990khvalynskiy], Khlopkov Bugor and collective flat-grave burials such as Maksimovka I on the Samara-Volga steppe margin [@tsibin2019maksimovka] document early herding (cattle, sheep, goats and horses) and Balkan-Carpathian copper exchange. Terrestrial-herbivore AMS dates place Khvalynsk I-II between 4508-4340 cal BC and 4346-4171 cal BC (2-sigma) [@vybornov2022khronologiya], with regional population reaching 21,5k by 4000BC.

### Bronze Age Villages and Sarmatian Nomads

During the Yamnaya (3300-2600 cal BC) and Middle Bronze Age Poltavka (2700-2100 cal BC) and Catacomb periods, mobile pastoralists using wheeled wagons expanded across the Saratov-Volgograd valleys, Yergeni Hills and Sarpa lakes [@shishlina2008reconstruction; @borisov2019palaeosols], lifting regional population from 33k (3000BC) to 54k around 2400BC before the 2200-2000 cal BC dry phase (when settlement contracted during the Lola period to 32k at 2000BC).

The transition from the Potapovka/Pokrovsk (1900-1700 cal BC) chariot-warrior burials to the Srubnaya (Timber-Grave) Culture (1700-1100 cal BC) [@malov2008nizhneye; @lopatin2014nachalo] produced a clear north-south contrast: the northern Saratov-Volgograd river valleys (60k km²) supported more than 850 permanent Srubnaya villages (*poseleniya*) with large timber-framed semi-subterranean houses (80-180 m², housing 62k mixed farmers and herders), whereas the southern Kalmyk and Astrakhan semi-deserts (185k km²) were used for seasonal dune camps (*stoyanki*, 33k mobile herders), giving a Late Bronze Age regional peak of 95k (78k-114k) at 1500BC (0,388 persons/km²).

In the Early Iron Age (600BC-400AD), studied by A. S. Skripkin [@skripkin2012chislennosti; @balabanova2015skripkin], V. M. Klepikov [@klepikov2002sarmaty] and M. V. Krivosheev, E. V. Pererva and M. V. Eltsov [@krivosheev2021chelovek], the Lower Volga passed from the Sauromatian (6th-4th c. BC, 65k) and Early Sarmatian (Prokhorovka, 4th-2nd c. BC, 82k at 300BC, followed by a mid-3rd-century BC dry-steppe pullback to 66k [@klepikov2002sarmaty]) periods to the Middle Sarmatian (Susly/Aorsi Confederacy, 1st c. BC-mid-2nd c. AD) expansion (Kosika, Verkhnoye Pogromnoye). In a dedicated demographic study, A. S. Skripkin [@skripkin2012chislennosti] compared Lower Volga Sarmatian burial densities against 18th- and 19th-century Kalmyk nomadic censuses (30k-45k *kibitkas*), showing that the Lower Volga pastures supported 65k-110k Sarmatian nomads (90k-97k midpoint in 1-150AD). Across more than 2,3k Lower Volga skeletons, M. A. Balabanova [@balabanova2000antropologiya; @balabanova2009khronologicheskiye; @balabanova2013detskaya] and E. V. Pererva and E. G. Zubareva [@pererva2015istorii] recorded high child mortality in Srubnaya (39,5%) and Early Sarmatian (34,8%) cemeteries, contrasted with the customary exclusion of children under 15 (only 4,5% of burials) and a strong excess of adult males (a male-to-female ratio of 2,15) in Late Sarmatian kurgans (Figure \ref{fig:volga-subsistence}B; Table \ref{tab:volga-bioarch}).

## Khazar Itil, Saksin, Golden Horde Cities and the Kalmyk Khanate

### Khazar Itil and Saksin

Following the post-Hunnic population low (43k at 400AD) and the Arab-Khazar war of 737AD, the Khazar Khagan transferred his court permanently to the Lower Volga Delta (Itil/Atil). At Semibugry and Barany Bugor (Семибугоринский археологический комплекс), excavated since 2020 by D. S. Solovyev, D. V. Vasilyev and E. E. Kravchenko [@solovyev2022semibugry] along the Bolda delta channel in Kamyzyaksky District, Astrakhan Oblast, a large 8th-10th century Khazar urban and suburban complex covers ~ 150 ha, yielding Saltovo-Mayaki amphorae, Khazar royal *tamga* bricks, an 8th-century Abbasid silver dirham and large brick foundations (estimated urban population 25k-40k).

Summarising 20 years of excavations (2000-2020) at Samosdelka (Самосдельское городище), D. V. Vasilyev [@vasilyev2015saksin; @vasilyev2020samosdelka] showed that the site (~ 150-200 ha across three delta islands) preserves a lower Khazar layer (9th-10th c. AD) with a triangular burnt-brick fortress and *yurt*-shaped dwellings (10k-18k inhabitants), sealed by a fire-and-flood layer from Sviatoslav's 965/969AD campaign. Together with Kalmyk-steppe outposts (Bashanta I-II [@ochirgoryaeva2020bashanta]) and floodplain herders, the Khazar Lower Volga reached 138k (115k-165k) at 900AD. In the 11th-early 13th centuries, the middle layer of Samosdelka flourished as the trading port of Saksin, where Abu Hamid al-Gharnati (1131-1153AD) described Oghuz, Bolgar, Suvar and Khazar quarters (matched directly to Samosdelka's four pottery traditions by Vasilyev [@vasilyev2015saksin]), supporting 15k-25k urban residents within a regional population of 104k at 1200AD.

### The Golden Horde Heartland on the Lower Volga

During the 1250s-1360s AD, the Lower Volga and Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain served as the personal domain of the Jochid Khans and the most heavily urbanised river corridor in Eastern Europe [@yegorov1985geografiya; @fyodorovdavydov1994goroda; @nedashkovsky2010goroda; @sitdikov2022volgoural] (Figure \ref{fig:volga-cities}). In the northern Saratov right-bank sector, Ukek (Uvekskoye Gorodishche, modern Saratov) stretched more than 3,5 km along the Volga across >205 ha with brick palaces, mosques, bathhouses (*hammams*) and Christian and Muslim quarters, housing 9k-10k urban residents [@nedashkovsky2000ukek; @nedashkovsky2010goroda]. Across its 420 km² rural district (*okruga*), L. F. Nedashkovsky and M. B. Shigapov [@nedashkovsky2010goroda; @nedashkovsky2022predmety; @nedashkovsky2022izdeliya; @shigapov2022selishch] mapped 53 rural settlements (3 satellite towns and 50 farming villages), exemplified by Bagaevskoye Selishche (5,1 ha, >90 cm cultural layer, excavated 2002-2021, yielding iron sickles, scythes, saws and fishhooks), which supported 12k-18k rural inhabitants. Further south at Dubovka, Beldzhamen/Bezdezh (Vodyanskoye Gorodishche) covered 50 ha (6k-9k inhabitants), with distinct Russian Christian, Volga Bolgar (stone mosque and baths) and Kipchak-Mongol quarters [@yegorov1985geografiya; @nedashkovsky2010goroda].

In the Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain, the 14th-century imperial capital of Sarai al-Jadid/Sarai Berke (Tsarevskoye Gorodishche, Leninsk) encompassed a compact urban core of >400 ha (~1,55k aristocratic house mounds) and a suburban estate belt of >1k-1,5k ha, surrounded by 17 satellite villages [@nedashkovsky2010goroda], supporting a 1340s population of 70k-100k inhabitants [@yegorov1985geografiya; @fyodorovdavydov1994goroda; @sitdikov2022volgoural]. Downstream at Kharabali, Sarai Batu/Sarai al-Mahrusa (Selitrennoye Gorodishche) and the royal necropolis of Ak-Sarai (Lapas) stretched 7-12 km along the Akhtuba across ~ 380-400 ha of dense urban quarters and ~ 1k ha of suburban estates and workshops (mapped in 2000-2020 by Yu. A. Zeleneev and E. M. Pigarev [@zeleneev2018selitrennom; @pigarev2021topografii]), housing 60k-75k inhabitants. In the Volga Delta, the Golden Horde port cities included Hajji-Tarkhan (Shareny Bugor, 150 ha, 18k-25k), Summerkent (Samosdelka upper layer, 80-100 ha, 6k-10k [@vasilyev2020samosdelka]) and Krasnoyarskoye/Moshayk (5k-10k).

At the height of the Golden Horde in 1340AD, Lower Volga towns housed 170k-230k inhabitants, supported by 50k-70k settled floodplain farmers and fishermen and 100k-140k steppe pastoralists - giving a regional total of 375k (308k-450k, 1,53 persons/km²). Between the Black Death (1346), the civil wars of the *Velikaya Zamyatnya* (1359-1380) and Timur's winter campaign of 1395-1396AD, the floodplain cities lost roughly four-fifths of their inhabitants, reducing the regional population to 87k in 1400AD.

### Astrakhan, the Nogais, the Kalmyks and Russian Fortresses

As shown by M. V. Moiseev [@moiseev2015stepnyye], I. V. Zaitsev [@zaitsev2006astrakhanskoye] and A. V. Syzranov [@syzranov2014astrakhani], the post-Jochid Astrakhan Khanate (1459-1556AD) centred at Hajji-Tarkhan supported an urban and semi-settled *Yurt* Tatar population of 15k-25k (fielding 3k cavalrymen), while V. V. Trepavlov [@trepavlov2016nogayskoy] established from Manghit *san* lists that the Western *uluses* of the Nogai Horde wintering along the Lower Volga numbered 80k-120k nomads in 1500-1550AD (regional total 130k at 1550AD). Immediately after Ivan IV's annexation of Astrakhan (1554-1556), civil war and the severe winter freeze (*dzhut*), famine and plague of 1557-1558 (witnessed at Astrakhan by Anthony Jenkinson in 1558) devastated the Nogai *uluses*, reducing the regional population to 68k by 1600AD [@trepavlov2016nogayskoy].

Between 1558 and 1700AD, two demographic movements reshaped the Lower Volga. First, the Russian garrison and *posad* network expanded along the river: Astrakhan (moved to Hare Island in 1558, stone Kremlin built 1582-1589) grew to 12k-16k permanent residents by 1700AD (including *streltsy*, Russian townspeople, Bukharan, Persian, Armenian and Indian merchant *dvory* and *Yurt* Tatar Muslim suburbs [@syzranov2014astrakhani]), alongside Saratov (1590, 4,5k-7k urban plus 6k rural settlers), Tsaritsyn (1589, 2,5k-4k), Chyorny Yar (1627), Krasny Yar (1667) and Dmitriyevsk (Kamyshin, 1668) (~34k total Russian and settled inhabitants). Second, beginning in 1628-1632, Western Mongol (Oirat - Torghut, Derbet and Khoshut) tribes under Tayishi Kho Orluk migrated into the Lower Volga steppes [@tepkeev2012kalmyki]. Under Ayuka Khan (r. 1669-1724, granted the title of Khan in 1690), reinforced by new Derbet and Dzungar arrivals studied by V. T. Tepkeev [@tepkeev2025dzhungarskiye] and N. L. Muzraev [@muzraev2025uchastiye], the Kalmyk Khanate numbered 35k-45k *kibitkas* (160k-210k Kalmyks, fielding 20k-40k horsemen) plus 20k subordinate Nogai and *Yurt* Tatars, lifting the Lower Volga region to 245k (210k-280k, 1 persons/km²) in 1700AD.

## Russian Peasant Settlement, the Volga Germans and the Kalmyk Steppe

Between 1700 and 1900AD, the Lower Volga was transformed from a pastoral frontier into one of Imperial Russia's major grain-exporting, fishing and river-shipping regions, expanding more than fourteen-fold from 245k (1700AD) to 3,65M by 1900AD (Figure \ref{fig:volga-holocene}B). Following the completion of the 60 km Tsaritsyn Defensive Line (*Tsaritsynskaya storozhevaya liniya*, 1718-1720) between the Volga and the Don and the establishment of the Dubovka Cossack Host (1734), Russian and Ukrainian state and landlord peasants settled the right-bank river valleys of Saratov and Kamyshin [@kabuzan1963narodonaseleniye; @solovyov2013saratovskoy; @brylyov2018volgogradskoy], lifting regional population to 390k by 1750AD. Under Catherine II's Manifestos of 1762 and 1763, analysed by I. R. Pleve [@pleve1998nemetskiye] and V. Dönninghaus [@doenninghaus2011nemetskikh], 25,6k-27k German colonists settled 104 mother colonies between 1764 and 1767 along the Saratov-Kamyshin right bank (*Bergseite*) and northern Trans-Volga left bank (*Wiesenseite*), while Moravian Brethren (Herrnhuter) founded Sarepta near Tsaritsyn in 1765.

In January 1771, Ubashi Khan led roughly 30k-33k left-bank Torghut and Khoshut *kibitkas* (~150k-170k people) eastwards out of the Lower Volga back towards Dzungaria, leaving only ~11k-13k right-bank Derbet and Torghut tents (~50k-60k Kalmyks) trapped west of the un-iced Volga [@ochirov2008tyurkoyazychnyye; @okonova2012migratsii; @kyshpanakov2026kalmyki]. This sudden depopulation of the Astrakhan Trans-Volga (Zavolzhye fell from 67k in 1750 to 28k in 1800AD, even as Saratov agricultural growth lifted the overall Lower Volga to 790k in 1800AD) prompted Paul I's decree of 11 March 1801 permitting Sultan Bukei Nuraliev to lead Junior Zhuz Kazakhs across the Ural into the Ryn Sands [@belousov2019bukeyevskoy]. By 1850AD, the Inner (Bukey) Kazakh Horde (~100k-120k Kazakhs centred at Khanskaya Stavka), state-peasant salt-carters (*chumaki*) at Lakes Elton and Baskunchak and rapid natural increase among the Volga Germans (reaching 165k by 1850) and Saratov peasantry raised the regional total to 1,88M (7,67 persons/km²) [@kabuzan1963narodonaseleniye; @doenninghaus2011nemetskikh; @belousov2019bukeyevskoy].

After the Emancipation of 1861, the opening of the Gryazi-Tsaritsyn (1871), Ryazan-Ural (1871-1894, linking Saratov and Pokrovskaya Sloboda) and Baskunchak (1882) railways and the rise of Nobel Brothers' oil-tanker fleets at Astrakhan and Tsaritsyn, the First All-Russian Census of 28 January 1897 [@troynitsky1904saratov; @troynitsky1904astrakhan] provides a comprehensive count across the five Lower Volga regions. In the Saratov-Volgograd Valley Corridor (60k km²), Saratov Governorate recorded 2,41M inhabitants in 1897 [@troynitsky1904saratov; @solovyov2013saratovskoy]; within the Lower Volga river and northern Trans-Volga districts (Saratov, Kamyshin, Tsaritsyn uplands, Volsk, Khvalynsk, Atkarsk and the Volga German canton of Novouzensk and Nikolayevsk uyezds [@brylyov2018volgogradskoy; @doenninghaus2011nemetskikh]), population reached 2,18M by 1900AD, including ~390k-405k Volga Germans across mother and daughter colonies and the cities of Saratov (137,1k in 1897), Kamyshin (16,3k), Volsk (27,1k), Khvalynsk (15,1k) and Dubovka (16,3k). In the Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain (18k km²), anchored by the railway and timber hub of Tsaritsyn (55,2k in 1897, up from 6,7k in 1861 [@brylyov2018volgogradskoy]), Tsarev (6,9k), Chyorny Yar (4,2k), Yenotayevsk (2,8k), Vladimirovka and dense Russian, Ukrainian and Mordvinian orchard and fishery villages along the Akhtuba, population reached 410k in 1900AD.

In the Volga Delta and north-western Caspian coast (22k km²), Astrakhan Governorate recorded 1M inhabitants in 1897 [@troynitsky1904astrakhan], and the delta proper (Astrakhan uyezd 219,8k and Krasny Yar uyezd 66k, plus seasonal fishery workers and delta Tatar villages [@pirova2020tatarakh]) reached 380k by 1900AD, led by Astrakhan city (112,9k permanent residents in 1897, swelling by >100k seasonal fishermen and dockers each spring). In the Kalmyk Steppe and Yergeni Hills (75k km²), analysed in detail by L. V. Okonova [@okonova2012migratsii], U. B. Ochirov [@ochirov2008tyurkoyazychnyye] and V. A. Kyshpanakov [@kyshpanakov2026kalmyki], the Kalmyk Steppe (*Kalmytskaya step*) of Astrakhan Governorate counted 128,6k nomadic Kalmyks plus ~10k Russian and Ukrainian settlers (total 138,6k in the steppe proper), alongside peasant road-villages (*traktovye syola*) along the Yergeni ridge (Elista, Remontnoye and Kresty) and Sarepta, giving 190k across the 75k km² region in 1900AD. Finally, in the Astrakhan-Volgograd Trans-Volga and Ryn Steppe (70k km²), the Inner (Bukey) Kazakh Horde counted 214,8k inhabitants in 1897 (96,5% Kazakhs, plus sedentary trading settlements at Khanskaya Stavka, Talovka and Novaia Kazanka studied by S. S. Belousov [@belousov2019bukeyevskoy]), which together with the Baskunchak and Elton salt-mining towns and the southern Trans-Volga *volosts* of Tsarev and Novouzensk uyezds totalled 490k in 1900AD (regional total 3,65M, density 14,9 persons/km²).

# Limitations

Three practical constraints affect Lower Volga population estimates. First, multi-metre Holocene rises and falls of the Caspian Sea (the Mangyshlak lowstand around 8000BC, the Novocaspian highstands and the 10th- and 14th-century rises) flooded or eroded delta sites (such as the Samosdelka fire-and-flood layer [@vasilyev2020samosdelka]), while shifting Volga and Akhtuba river channels have washed away parts of Ukek, Beldzhamen and Selitrennoye [@nedashkovsky2010goroda; @pigarev2021topografii]. Second, historians and archaeologists still debate how much the twin Golden Horde capitals of Sarai Batu (Selitrennoye) and Sarai al-Jadid (Tsarevskoye) overlapped in population during the 1330s-1360s AD [@yegorov1985geografiya; @zeleneev2018selitrennom; @sitdikov2022volgoural]; our 1340AD floodplain estimate (195k) allows for a partial transfer of residents between the two capitals rather than adding both at their peak sizes. Third, the Nogai Horde (15th-16th c.), the Kalmyk Khanate (17th-18th c.) and the Inner Bukey Kazakh Horde (19th c.) all moved camp seasonally across the Ural, Lower Volga and Kuma-Manych steppes [@trepavlov2016nogayskoy; @tepkeev2025dzhungarskiye; @belousov2019bukeyevskoy], while late 19th-century Astrakhan and Tsaritsyn drew more than 150k seasonal spring and summer fishery and dock workers who were absent in January when the 1897 census was taken [@troynitsky1904astrakhan]. Our figures count only the permanent residents of the 245k km² study area.

# Conclusion

Across the Holocene, the Lower Volga swung repeatedly between open-steppe herding and dense river-valley town life. After early farming and nomadic growth during the Late Bronze Age Srubnaya village expansion (95k at 1500BC) and the Middle Sarmatian Aorsi confederacy (97k at 150AD), the Volga Delta and Volga-Akhtuba Floodplain twice served as the centre of large steppe empires. Under the Khazar Khaganate, growth at Itil (Semibugry and Samosdelka) lifted the regional population to 138k in 900AD, followed by Pre-Mongol Saksin at 104k in 1200AD; under the Golden Horde, the cities of Sarai al-Jadid, Sarai Batu, Ukek, Beldzhamen and Hajji-Tarkhan carried the region to a medieval peak of 375k in 1340AD. After Timur destroyed the floodplain cities in 1395AD and famine and plague struck the Nogais in 1557-1558 (68k in 1600AD), 17th-century Oirat-Kalmyk migration (35k-45k tents under Ayuka Khan) and Russian fortress towns at Astrakhan, Saratov and Tsaritsyn brought the population back to 245k by 1700AD. Even after ~150k-170k left-bank Kalmyks departed for Dzungaria in 1771, Russian peasant and Volga German settlement of the Saratov-Kamyshin valleys, the arrival of the Inner (Bukey) Kazakh Horde in 1801 and late 19th-century railway and river trade raised the Lower Volga population to 3,65M (14,9 persons/km²) by 1900AD.
